title: Research
text:
Bayesian variable selection with spike-and-slab priors gives a probability that each predictor belongs in the model. Markov chain Monte Carlo is slow when there are thousands of predictors, so variational Bayes (VB) is used instead. Standard VB has two weak points in this setting: its results depend strongly on the prior settings, and its predictions are often poorly calibrated, i.e. they are biased toward the mean. My dissertation, with Dr. Alexander McLain, develops VB methods that stay fast and fix these problems.

Parameter expanded VB for spike-and-slab linear regression. Preprint on Research Square; under review at Statistics and Computing. Software: spexvb on CRAN.
Parameter exploded VB for sparse high-dimensional linear regression. In preparation.
VB for scalar-on-function regression. In progress. The predictor is a curve, such as a day of accelerometer data, expanded in a basis. This project carries the ideas of the first two projects to functional predictors.



The first figure below shows the calibration problem with simulated data. In panel (a), the predictions from standard VB are pulled toward zero, because the points lie on a flatter line than the 45° line. In panel (b), the calibration coefficient αc (black line; αc ≈ 1 means good calibration) and the MSE (gray line) both change with the prior precision τb. So, the user of standard VB must choose τb well to get good predictions.
Our method, spexvb, adds parameter expansion to VB. The second figure compares how much the test-set MSE changes across five values of τb. We see that the range for spexvb (red) is much smaller than for sparsevb (black), the standard VB method, in every scenario. So, spexvb depends much less on the prior setting.






Standard VB with simulated data: (a) true versus estimated E(y) for √τb = 3.3; (b) calibration coefficient αc (solid black), MSE (solid gray, rescaled), and the difference between the estimated and true number of non-zero coefficients (dashed) by √τb.







Range (maximum minus minimum) of test-set MSE over τb1/2 ∈ {1/20, 1/4, 1, 4, 20}, n = 200, by number of groups with non-zero signals; centers are means and whiskers ±1 SD.





Figures from Olejua, Saha, Ghosal, Bai, and McLain (2025), Research Square preprint, licensed CC BY 4.0.



The methods are evaluated with factorial simulation studies on a high-performance computing cluster, and applied to genomic and wearable data.

title: Research
text:
Wearable and accelerometer data

Clustering 24-hour physical activity in young children. We clustered hourly activity curves of children 6 to 36 months old with model-based functional clustering. Pediatric Exercise Science, 2025 (first author).
Non-wear imputation in GGIR. We measured the bias of GGIR’s non-wear imputation by imposing real non-wear patterns on complete wrist accelerometer recordings. Along the way, two of my fixes were merged into the GGIR package.
Walking and cognition in Parkinson’s disease. Longitudinal mixed models of changes in walking and cognition by motor subtype. Parkinsonism & Related Disorders, 2026 (first author).

title: Research
text:
High-dimensional mixed models

lmmprobe fits sparse high-dimensional linear mixed models with a partitioned empirical Bayes ECM algorithm, developed by Dr. Anja Zgodic and co-authors (Statistics and Computing, 2025). My contribution was to the software: I optimized the R package by rewriting its core routines in C++ with OpenMP.

title: Research
text:
Before the Ph.D.
From 2018 to 2021 I was the biostatistician of the research office at Hospital Universitario San Ignacio in Bogotá. I built clinical prediction models (emergency room mortality, high-flow nasal cannula failure in COVID-19 pneumonia), designed patient registries in REDCap, and co-authored papers in cardiology, infectious disease, and pulmonology. Before that I spent about seven years in banking and consulting, building credit scoring and money-laundering risk models.

title: Peter Olejua
text:
I am on the job market for postdoctoral and research scientist positions starting in 2027. If my work fits your group, please get in touch.
I am a Ph.D. candidate in Biostatistics at the Arnold School of Public Health, University of South Carolina, advised by Dr. Alexander McLain. I expect to graduate in May 2027. I live in the Dallas–Fort Worth area of Texas.
My work is in functional data analysis and scalable Bayesian methods. Wearable devices record activity minute by minute, for days or weeks, so each person gives a curve instead of a single number. I develop and apply methods that use the whole curve, and I write them as software that other people can use.

title: Peter Olejua
text:
What I work on


Variational Bayes for high-dimensional regression
Fast Bayesian variable selection with spike-and-slab priors that keeps the uncertainty honest. R package spexvb on CRAN.


Scalar-on-function regression
Bayesian regression where the predictor is a curve, for example 24-hour activity from a wrist accelerometer.


Wearable and accelerometer data
Clustering 24-hour activity patterns, processing raw accelerometer data with GGIR, and measuring the bias of non-wear imputation.

title: Peter Olejua
text:
Where I am going
I want to see statistical methods used in the world, not only published. My goal is to work with functional data from wearable devices, developing methods and applying my own methods and those of others, so that practitioners can use them. That can happen in academia or in a company that builds wearable devices. More in my own words.

title: In my words
text:
Where do you come from?
I am the son of Venezuelan and Colombian parents. I studied mathematics at Universidad Simón Bolívar in Caracas, and I grew up between two cultures, which helps me understand people who see things differently.


How did you get from mathematics to health?
I spent about ten years applying mathematics to real problems. First in banking, measuring credit risk and screening for money laundering. Then I moved to health: I did a master’s in biostatistics in Bogotá and worked as the biostatistician of a university hospital, through the COVID-19 pandemic.


What do you work on now?
Functional data from wearable devices. A wrist accelerometer records how a person moves, minute by minute, for days. Each person gives a curve, not a number. I work on Bayesian methods that can use the whole curve and still run fast, and I write them as R packages so that other people can use them.


Where do you see yourself in five years?
I want to see the impact of research in the world. Many methods are published and then not used. I would like my methods to be used by practitioners, and I would like to apply good methods, mine or someone else’s, to real problems. That can be in academia or in a company that builds wearable devices. Functional data is an active field, with a lot still to develop, and that is what I want to keep doing.


Who shaped you as a researcher?
My advisor, Dr. Alexander McLain. As I said in my USC profile:

What I admire most about Dr. McLain is his remarkable ability to adapt to anyone at their level in order to help them complete their research. He possesses a unique talent for breaking down complex concepts, providing guidance that is tailored to individual needs, and fostering an environment where curiosity and intellectual growth thrive.



And outside work?
I dance Kizomba, ride my bicycle, and go hiking with my wife and our dog.

Read the full story: I Am Public Health: Peter Olejua, Arnold School of Public Health, September 2025.

title: Software
text:
Contributions
GGIR is the R package for processing raw accelerometer data. Two of my pull requests were merged in July 2026:

#1522: fixed an NA/NaN error in g.impute() (non-wear imputation) when a study dates file is used, and the date handling in check_log().
#1523: fixed activity-log (qwindow) segments that were assigned one day early.
